content: Health initiatives must address broader health information needs and be guided by a comprehensive strategy that integrates leadership, financial, organizational, human, and technological resources. This strategy should form the foundation for a detailed and costed action plan that facilitates coordination among multiple stakeholders. Digital health initiatives should be governed by robust governance structures that span across various health priorities. These structures must be supported by standards and an architecture that ensures seamless integration. Digital health solutions should be developed with principles of transparency, accessibility, scalability, replicability, interoperability, privacy, security, and confidentiality. While digitization offers significant advantages and benefits, it also introduces inherent risks to the security, confidentiality, and interoperability of data used in healthcare services. All individual-level health data must be classified as sensitive personal data or personally identifiable information, necessitating a high standard of safety and security. Consequently, a strong legal and regulatory framework is essential to protect privacy, confidentiality, data integrity, availability, and the processing of personal health data. Additionally, the system must address cybersecurity, trust-building, accountability, governance, ethics, equity, capacity building, and digital literacy. This ensures the collection and sharing of high-quality data to support the planning and transformation of health services. The development of these guidelines involved WHO staff and consultants who reviewed recent global and regional guidance documents, conducted consultative meetings, and incorporated inputs from technical experts. The minimum datasets and priority indicators included in the guidelines were identified through consultations with technical experts from country-level, regional, and global perspectives. The Core Advisory Group, responsible for overseeing the development of the guidelines, included co-chairs and members with expertise in strategic information, monitoring, and evaluation (M&E). It also included representatives from WHO regions, Member States (health ministries), civil society, partners, and academic institutions. This group provided inputs on the overall approach to the guidance and indicators and reviewed drafts of the chapters at various stages. For each program area, a technical working group was established, comprising co-chairs, WHO technical staff, and members representing health ministries, non-governmental and academic partners, program implementers, civil society, and development partner agencies. These agencies included UNAIDS, UNICEF, the United States President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria. The technical working groups, which met virtually, focused on prioritizing and organizing programmatic sections, minimum datasets, and indicators to align with the latest programmatic recommendations. WHO headquarters provided overall direction, coordination, and oversight. All external contributors to the development of the guidelines completed a WHO declaration of interests form. The guidelines are organized into six technical chapters covering person-centered HIV prevention monitoring, HIV patient monitoring for testing, early diagnosis, and treatment, integrating related infections into HIV surveillance systems, leveraging routine data for HIV surveillance, digital health data, and strengthening data use. Each chapter includes a brief description of critical measurement issues, reasons for selecting the data elements in the minimum dataset, and priority indicators for that program area. References to published materials are also provided for operationalizing the collection and use of these data. Chapter 8 contains detailed metadata for priority and core indicators, including those derived from programmatic data and surveys. Web annexes to the guidelines include a complete minimum dataset across all program areas in Excel format for direct use (Web Annex A) and a list of additional indicators that can be considered based on programmatic needs and context (Web Annex B). Web Annexes C–M are specific to the chapter on person-centered HIV patient monitoring for testing, early diagnosis, and treatment and can be used directly or adapted to country contexts. The intended audience for these guidelines includes national and subnational HIV program managers, surveillance officers, partners, and other stakeholders involved in the design and use of M&E systems, surveillance, and tools for collecting, analyzing, and using HIV health sector data. This includes national-level staff responsible for establishing strategic information policies, guidelines, frameworks, tools, and health information systems (HIS), as well as staff involved in data collection, analysis, and use at national, subnational, and service delivery levels (facility and community) to monitor and improve programs. The guidelines will also be of interest and use to technical partners and other stakeholders supporting the design and implementation of HIV health sector M&E systems and related tools. Other potential users include stakeholders involved in developing and analyzing strategic information, such as non-governmental organizations (NGOs), private-sector care providers, civil society organizations, and academic groups engaged in teaching and research.
